surveyDefinition.title: Mattresses — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on purchase journey, decision drivers, product requirements, and satisfaction/churn signals.

segments.name: Comfort-Focused Buyers
segments.description: Buyers who prioritize comfort and support above all else, often due to pain or sleep quality concerns. They are willing to pay more for specialized materials and features that promise better sleep.

segments.name: Value-Driven Shoppers
segments.description: Buyers who weigh price against quality and durability, seeking the best long-term value. They research extensively, compare prices, and are likely to wait for sales or use financing.

segments.name: Health & Eco-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Buyers who are motivated by health benefits and environmental impact, preferring organic, non-toxic, and sustainable materials. They are willing to pay a premium for certified products.

segments.name: Tech-Savvy Innovators
segments.description: Buyers who are attracted to smart features, cooling technology, and adjustable bases. They are early adopters and value innovation and convenience over tradition.

segments.name: Practical Replacers
segments.description: Buyers who purchase out of necessity, often replacing an old or worn mattress. They are less engaged with the category, prefer simple and affordable options, and are not swayed by premium features.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Mattresses buyers in North America. It asks how people use Mattresses, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Mattresses for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who have purchased a mattress in the last 12 months or plan to within the next 6 months; Primary decision-maker for the mattress purchase; Ages 25-64. Excluded: Business buyers (hotels, hospitals, rental properties); Children under 18; Those who have never purchased or plan to purchase a mattress.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Household consumers buy mattresses for personal use, pay for them out of pocket (or via financing), and decide which mattress to purchase, typically after in-store or online research. While businesses like hotels also buy mattresses, the dominant consumer market is clear and the category is widely recognized as B2C.
respondentBehaviours: Research online before purchase (reviews, comparison sites)
Consider factors like comfort, firmness, durability, price, and warranty
May use financing or buy during promotional periods
Increasingly open to online mattress-in-a-box purchases
Value sleep quality and health benefits
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Sleep Context & Usage Profile
sections.covers: Establish the respondent's sleep environment, household composition, and the role they play in mattress decisions.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Trace the path from need recognition to purchase, including triggers, research, channels, and the factors that ultimately decide the choice.

sections.label: Product Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Capture must-have attributes, quality cues, and the trade-offs buyers are willing to make between features, price, and brand.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Replacement Intent
sections.covers: Measure satisfaction with the current mattress, identify friction points, and gauge likelihood to recommend and repurchase.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's current sleep context and household, then moves through the purchase journey from trigger to decision, explores product requirements and trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction and future intent. This arc allows the segmentation model to distinguish buyers by their primary job-to-be-done (comfort, value, health, tech, or practicality) and their price sensitivity, while covering the category's essential topics of firmness, temperature, motion isolation, trial, warranty, and price.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Mattresses in North America — who Adults who have purchased a mattress in the last 12 months or plan to within the next 6 months; Primary decision-maker for the mattress purchase; Ages 25-64. This ensures the survey captures relevant attitudes and behaviors.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'bb1' (What first made you decide to start looking for a new mattress?) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it captures the respondent's own stated trigger for entering the market, cleanly separating necessity-driven practical replacers from pain-driven comfort prioritizers, upgrade-driven tech innovators, and value-driven researchers.
notes: Weights are assigned only to options that clearly discriminate; many options (e.g., mattress age, household composition, size, satisfaction levels) are left unscored because they do not uniquely identify a segment.
Each segment has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.

Some options point to multiple segments when the behaviour genuinely overlaps (e.g., giving up eco-friendly materials signals tech innovators but also value optimizers; here we assigned to the most distinctive segment).
The tie-break question is bb1 because it is the first self-reported reason for shopping, which is the most direct behavioural signal of segment membership.
4 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's current sleep context and household, then moves through the purchase journey from trigger to decision, explores product requirements and trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction and future intent. This arc allows the segmentation model to distinguish buyers by their primary job-to-be-done (comfort, value, health, tech, or practicality) and their price sensitivity, while covering the category's essential topics of firmness, temperature, motion isolation, trial, warranty, and price.
storyline_notes: Replaced the generic 'usage frequency' beat with 'sleep quality and pain points' because mattress usage is constant; the meaningful variation is in the need state and physical issues.
Added a dedicated beat on 'trial period and warranty' as these are critical trust signals in the mattress category, especially for online purchases.
Included 'sleep environment and household' to capture couple dynamics and room constraints, which are key differentiators for the 'Couple Compromise Seeker' persona.
The 'purchase journey' section emphasizes research and channel because North American buyers are known to research online before purchase, and the rise of mattress-in-a-box is a key market trend.
The 'product requirements' section includes trade-offs and value perception to separate price-sensitive segments from those willing to pay for premium features.
The final section on satisfaction and replacement intent captures churn risk and future loyalty, which is essential for a durable good with a long replacement cycle.
metadata.classification_reason: Household consumers buy mattresses for personal use, pay for them out of pocket (or via financing), and decide which mattress to purchase, typically after in-store or online research. While businesses like hotels also buy mattresses, the dominant consumer market is clear and the category is widely recognized as B2C.
